report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is not supported: capsaicin has **not been shown to treat breast cancer in humans**. It should not replace established breast-cancer therapy.

**What supports the idea:** Laboratory research is biologically interesting. Capsaicin reduced viability, migration, and/or induced cell-cycle arrest or apoptosis in cultured human breast-cancer cell lines, including MDA-MB-231. TRPV1 (a capsaicin-responsive receptor) is present and functional in some breast-cancer cells, offering a plausible mechanism. But these are *in-vitro* findings at controlled concentrations—not evidence that eating chili peppers, taking supplements, or using capsaicin products treats a tumor in a person.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33173974/  
https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0179950

**Critical limitations / contrary evidence:** A peer-reviewed review concludes that the clinical value of oral capsaicin as an adjunct to chemotherapy remains speculative. Systemic dosing is also problematic: doses sufficient for anticancer effects may cause acute pain and neurologic inflammation. Reviews discuss both anticancer and potentially tumor-promoting findings depending on model and conditions, underscoring that the biology is not settled.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10177684/

**What human evidence does exist:** Capsaicin skin patches have been studied for pain—such as chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy or pain after breast-cancer surgery—not for shrinking or curing breast cancer. Memorial Sloan Kettering likewise characterizes breast-cancer evidence as cell-line research and notes only a small pain-relief study in people.  
https://www.mskcc.org/cancer-care/integrative-medicine/herbs/capsaicin

If you have breast cancer, discuss any capsaicin supplement or alternative regimen with your oncology team; do not delay surgery, radiation, endocrine therapy, chemotherapy, or targeted treatment for it.
